title: Transport in Plants
description: Grade 11 Biology: means of transport in plants — diffusion, osmosis and water potential, the absorption and ascent of water by transpiration, and translocation of food.

topics.title: Means of Transport: Diffusion, Osmosis and Water Potential
topics.concept:
Plants need to move water, minerals and food from one part to another. Over short distances, substances move by diffusion — the movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration, without using energy. Diffusion is passive and slow, useful only for short-distance transport (for example, gases moving in and out of cells).

When carrier proteins help molecules cross a membrane down their concentration gradient without energy, it is facilitated diffusion. When molecules are pumped against their gradient using ATP, it is active transport.

Osmosis is a special kind of diffusion: the movement of water molecules across a semi-permeable membrane from a region of higher water concentration (dilute solution) to a region of lower water concentration (concentrated solution). The direction and rate of osmosis depend on both pressure and the concentration of solutes, summed up as water potential.

  • Pure water has the highest water potential (taken as zero).
  • Adding solute lowers the water potential (makes it negative).
  • Water always moves from higher to lower water potential.

Depending on the surrounding solution, a cell may be in a hypotonic solution (water enters, cell swells — turgid), an isotonic solution (no net movement), or a hypertonic solution (water leaves, the cell shrinks — plasmolysis).

examples.solution:
It is a special case of diffusion.

  • Osmosis is the movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane.
  • It goes from higher water concentration (dilute) to lower (concentrated).
examples.answer: Osmosis is the movement of water molecules across a semi-permeable membrane from a dilute to a more concentrated solution.

examples.problem: Example 2: What happens to a plant cell placed in a hypertonic (very concentrated) solution?
examples.solution:
Compare water potentials.

  • Water leaves the cell because the outside has lower water potential.
  • The cell shrinks — this is plasmolysis.
examples.answer: Water leaves the cell and it shrinks (plasmolysis).

examples.problem: Example 3: How does active transport differ from diffusion?
examples.solution:
Consider energy and direction.

  • Diffusion is passive (no energy), moving down the gradient.
  • Active transport uses ATP to move substances against the gradient.
examples.answer: Diffusion is passive and goes down the concentration gradient; active transport uses energy (ATP) to move substances against the gradient.

recap:
• Diffusion: passive movement high→low concentration; short distances only.
  • Facilitated diffusion (carrier, no energy) vs active transport (ATP, against gradient).
  • Osmosis: water across a semi-permeable membrane, dilute→concentrated.
  • Water potential: pure water = 0; solutes lower it; water moves high→low. Turgid / isotonic / plasmolysed.

quiz.q: Movement of water across a semi-permeable membrane is:
quiz.explanation: Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a semi-permeable membrane.

quiz.q: Active transport differs from diffusion because it:
quiz.explanation: Active transport uses ATP to move substances against the gradient.

topics.title: Absorption and Ascent of Water; Transpiration
topics.concept:
Water and dissolved minerals are absorbed mainly by the root hairs — thin extensions of root epidermal cells that hugely increase the surface area. Water enters by osmosis and then moves across the root toward the centre, where it reaches the water-conducting tissue, the xylem.

From the roots, water travels all the way up to the leaves through the xylem — this is the ascent of sap. In a tall tree this is a rise of many metres, achieved without any pump. The main driving force is the transpiration pull, explained by the cohesion–tension theory:

  • Transpiration — the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of the plant, mostly through tiny pores in the leaves called stomata — pulls water upward.
  • Cohesion — water molecules stick to one another (by hydrogen bonds), forming a continuous column.
  • Adhesion — water molecules stick to the walls of the narrow xylem vessels.

Together, the pull at the top and the unbroken, cohesive water column drag water up the xylem like a rope being pulled from above.

Each stoma is bordered by two guard cells that open the pore when turgid and close it when flaccid, controlling how much water is lost. Although transpiration loses a lot of water, it also helps absorb and transport water and minerals and cools the plant (a kind of evaporative cooling).

examples.problem: Example 1: Which tissue carries water from the roots to the leaves?
examples.solution:
There are two transport tissues.

  • Water (and minerals) travels in the xylem.
  • (Food travels in the phloem.)
examples.answer: The xylem carries water and minerals upward from the roots to the leaves.

examples.problem: Example 2: What is transpiration pull and why is it important?
examples.solution:
Loss of water creates a pull.

  • Transpiration (loss of water vapour from leaves) creates a suction that pulls the water column up.
  • It is the main force for the ascent of sap.
examples.answer: Transpiration pull is the suction created by water loss from leaves; it is the main force lifting water up the xylem.

examples.problem: Example 3: Name two benefits of transpiration besides being unavoidable.
examples.solution:
Transpiration is more than just water loss.

  • It helps absorb and transport water and minerals.
  • It cools the plant (evaporative cooling).
examples.answer: It helps transport water and minerals, and it cools the plant.

recap:
• Root hairs absorb water and minerals (large surface area); water enters by osmosis.
  • Water rises in the xylem (ascent of sap), driven by transpiration pull.
  • Cohesion–tension: cohesion + adhesion keep an unbroken water column; the pull lifts it.
  • Stomata (with guard cells) control transpiration; benefits = transport of water/minerals + cooling.

quiz.q: The chief force responsible for the upward movement of water in tall trees is:
quiz.explanation: Transpiration pull (cohesion–tension) is the main force lifting water.

quiz.q: Water is mostly lost from the plant through pores called:
quiz.explanation: Most transpiration occurs through stomata in the leaves.

topics.title: Translocation of Food (Phloem Transport)
topics.concept:
The food made in the leaves by photosynthesis (mainly the sugar sucrose) must be carried to all other parts of the plant — growing tips, fruits, seeds and storage organs like roots and tubers. This transport of food is called translocation, and it takes place through the phloem.

Unlike water in the xylem (which moves only upward), food in the phloem can move in any direction — up or down — from a region where it is made or stored (the source) to a region where it is used or stored (the sink). For example, leaves are a source in summer, while a growing fruit is a sink; a storage root can be a sink while filling and a source when sprouting.

The widely accepted explanation is the pressure-flow (mass-flow) hypothesis:

  • At the source, sugar is actively loaded into the phloem; this lowers the water potential, so water enters from the nearby xylem by osmosis, raising the pressure.
  • At the sink, sugar is removed (used or stored); water leaves, lowering the pressure.
  • The pressure difference pushes the sugary sap by bulk flow from the high-pressure source to the low-pressure sink.

Because loading sugar at the source needs energy, translocation in the phloem is an active process, unlike the passive ascent of water in the xylem.

examples.problem: Example 1: Which tissue translocates food, and what is the main substance transported?
examples.solution:
Recall the two conducting tissues.

  • Food is transported by the phloem.
  • The main substance is sucrose (sugar).
examples.answer: The phloem translocates food, mainly as sucrose.

examples.problem: Example 2: How does the direction of transport in the phloem differ from that in the xylem?
examples.solution:
Compare the two tissues.

  • Xylem moves water only upward.
  • Phloem can move food in any direction (source to sink).
examples.answer: Xylem transport is one-way (upward); phloem can move food in any direction, from source to sink.

examples.problem: Example 3: In the pressure-flow hypothesis, why does water enter the phloem at the source?
examples.solution:
Loading sugar changes water potential.

  • Sugar is loaded into the phloem at the source.
  • This lowers the water potential, so water enters by osmosis, raising pressure.
examples.answer: Loading sugar lowers the water potential at the source, so water enters by osmosis and raises the pressure.

recap:
• Translocation = transport of food (mainly sucrose) through the phloem.
  • Moves in any direction, from source to sink.
  • Pressure-flow hypothesis: load sugar at source → water in → high pressure; unload at sink → water out → low pressure; bulk flow source→sink.
  • It is an active process (loading needs energy), unlike the passive xylem ascent.

quiz.q: Translocation of food in plants occurs through the:
quiz.explanation: The phloem transports food (sucrose) from source to sink.

quiz.q: In the pressure-flow hypothesis, food moves from:
quiz.explanation: Food flows from a high-pressure source to a low-pressure sink.

questions.q: Movement of molecules from higher to lower concentration without energy is:
questions.explanation: Diffusion is passive movement down a concentration gradient.

questions.q: Osmosis is the movement of water across a:
questions.explanation: Osmosis occurs across a semi-permeable membrane.

questions.q: Pure water has a water potential of:
questions.explanation: Pure water has the highest water potential, taken as zero.

questions.q: A plant cell in a hypertonic solution undergoes:
questions.explanation: Water leaves the cell, causing it to shrink (plasmolysis).

questions.q: Transport that uses ATP to move substances against the gradient is:
questions.explanation: Active transport uses energy to move against the gradient.

questions.q: Water and minerals are mainly absorbed by:
questions.explanation: Root hairs absorb most water and minerals.

questions.q: Water rises from roots to leaves through the:
questions.explanation: The xylem carries water upward (ascent of sap).

questions.q: The main force for the ascent of sap in tall trees is:
questions.explanation: Transpiration pull (cohesion–tension) drives the ascent of sap.

questions.q: Most transpiration takes place through the:
questions.explanation: Stomata in leaves are the main site of transpiration.

questions.q: Stomatal opening and closing is controlled by:
questions.explanation: Turgid guard cells open the stoma; flaccid ones close it.

questions.q: Besides water loss, transpiration also:
questions.explanation: Transpiration cools the plant and aids transport of water and minerals.

questions.q: Transport of food in plants is called:
questions.explanation: Translocation is the transport of food through the phloem.

questions.q: Food is translocated mainly as:
questions.explanation: Sucrose is the main form in which food is transported.

questions.q: Unlike the xylem, the phloem can transport food:
questions.explanation: Phloem moves food in any direction, from source to sink.

questions.q: The accepted mechanism of phloem transport is the:
questions.explanation: The pressure-flow (mass-flow) hypothesis explains phloem transport.

questions.q: If a cell's water potential is more negative than its surroundings, water will:
questions.explanation: Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) potential — so it enters the cell.

questions.q: Wilting of a plant on a hot day happens because the rate of transpiration:
options: Exceeds the rate of water absorption
questions.explanation: When water loss outpaces uptake, cells lose turgor and the plant wilts.

questions.q: A continuous, unbroken water column in the xylem is maintained by:
questions.explanation: Hydrogen-bond cohesion keeps the water column unbroken as it is pulled up.

questions.q: A storage root that is filling with sugar acts as a ____, but when it sprouts it acts as a ____.
questions.explanation: While storing sugar it is a sink; when sprouting it exports sugar, becoming a source.

questions.q: Translocation in the phloem is an active process mainly because:
options: Loading sugar at the source requires energy
questions.explanation: Active loading of sugar at the source uses ATP, making translocation energy-dependent.

questions.q: Ringing (removing a ring of bark including phloem) causes the bark above the ring to swell because:
options: Sugars accumulate above the cut as downward transport is blocked
questions.explanation: Removing phloem blocks downward food transport, so sugars build up and the bark swells above the ring.
